title: 226. Algebra, Equations & Inequalities: Parameter Conditions for Positive Quadratic Roots
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2-kx+4=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2-kx+4=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation: For \(x^2-kx+4=0\), the sum of the roots is \(k\) and the product is \(4>0\). For both roots to be positive, the sum must be positive, so \(k>0\). The discriminant must also be nonnegative: \(k^2-16\ge0\), so \(k\le -4\) or \(k\ge4\). Intersecting with \(k>0\) gives \(k\ge4\).
questions.hint: Require a positive sum, a positive product, and a nonnegative discriminant.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2+kx+9=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2+kx+9=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation: For \(x^2+kx+9=0\), the sum of the roots is \(-k\) and the product is \(9>0\). For both roots to be positive, the sum must be positive, so \(-k>0\), meaning \(k<0\). The discriminant must be nonnegative: \(k^2-36\ge0\), so \(k\le -6\) or \(k\ge6\). Intersecting with \(k<0\) gives \(k\le -6\).
questions.hint: Use the sum of roots to determine the sign of \(k\), then apply the discriminant condition.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(2x^2-(k+1)x+2=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(2x^2-(k+1)x+2=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation:
The sum of the roots is \(\frac{k+1}{2}\), and the product is \(1>0\). For both roots to be positive, the sum must be positive, so \(k+1>0\), meaning \(k>-1\). The discriminant must be nonnegative:
\[
(k+1)^2-16\ge0
\]
This gives \(k+1\le -4\) or \(k+1\ge4\), so \(k\le -5\) or \(k\ge3\). Intersecting with \(k>-1\) gives \(k\ge3\).
questions.hint: Combine the positive-sum condition with the discriminant condition.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2-2kx+k^2-1=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2-2kx+k^2-1=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation: The sum of the roots is \(2k\), and the product is \(k^2-1\). For both roots to be positive, the sum must be positive, so \(k>0\). The product must be positive, so \(k^2-1>0\), giving \(k<-1\) or \(k>1\). Intersecting with \(k>0\) gives \(k>1\). The discriminant is \(4\), which is always positive, so no further restriction is needed.
questions.hint: Use the sum and product of roots, and note that the discriminant is always positive here.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2-(k+2)x+k=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2-(k+2)x+k=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation:
The sum of the roots is \(k+2\), and the product is \(k\). For both roots to be positive, the sum must be positive, so \(k+2>0\), meaning \(k>-2\). The product must be positive, so \(k>0\). The discriminant is
\[
(k+2)^2-4k=k^2+4>0
\]
which is always positive. Intersecting \(k>-2\) with \(k>0\) gives \(k>0\).
questions.hint: Combine the positive-sum and positive-product conditions; the discriminant is always positive here.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2+(k-3)x+k=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2+(k-3)x+k=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation:
The sum of the roots is \(3-k\), and the product is \(k\). For both roots to be positive, the sum must be positive, so \(k<3\), and the product must be positive, so \(k>0\). The discriminant is
\[
(k-3)^2-4k=k^2-10k+9=(k-1)(k-9)
\]
For real roots, \((k-1)(k-9)\ge0\), so \(k\le1\) or \(k\ge9\). Intersecting with \(0<k<3\) gives \(0<k\le1\).
questions.hint: Use the sum and product conditions first, then impose the discriminant condition.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2-(k+1)x+(k+2)=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2-(k+1)x+(k+2)=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation:
The sum of the roots is \(k+1\), and the product is \(k+2\). For both roots to be positive, \(k+1>0\) and \(k+2>0\), so \(k>-1\). The discriminant must be nonnegative:
\[
(k+1)^2-4(k+2)=k^2-2k-7\ge0
\]
Solving \(k^2-2k-7=0\) gives \(k=1\pm2\sqrt{2}\). Thus \(k\le1-2\sqrt{2}\) or \(k\ge1+2\sqrt{2}\). Intersecting with \(k>-1\) gives \(k\ge1+2\sqrt{2}\).
questions.hint: Combine the positivity conditions with the discriminant inequality and intersect the intervals.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2-(2k+1)x+(k^2+k)=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2-(2k+1)x+(k^2+k)=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation: The sum of the roots is \(2k+1\), and the product is \(k^2+k=k(k+1)\). For both roots to be positive, the sum must be positive, so \(k>-\frac{1}{2}\). The product must be positive, so \(k(k+1)>0\), giving \(k<-1\) or \(k>0\). Intersecting with \(k>-\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(k>0\). The discriminant is \(1\), which is always positive.
questions.hint: Use the positive-sum and positive-product conditions, and note the discriminant is always positive.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2-(k-2)x+(2k-3)=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2-(k-2)x+(2k-3)=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation:
The sum of the roots is \(k-2\), and the product is \(2k-3\). For both roots to be positive, \(k-2>0\) and \(2k-3>0\), so \(k>2\). The discriminant must be nonnegative:
\[
(k-2)^2-4(2k-3)=k^2-12k+16\ge0
\]
Solving \(k^2-12k+16=0\) gives \(k=6\pm2\sqrt{5}\). Thus \(k\le6-2\sqrt{5}\) or \(k\ge6+2\sqrt{5}\). Intersecting with \(k>2\) gives \(k\ge6+2\sqrt{5}\).
questions.hint: Require a positive sum, a positive product, and a nonnegative discriminant, then intersect the intervals.

questions.concept: Parameter condition for both roots of a quadratic to be positive
questions.learningObjective: Determine the range of \(k\) for \(x^2-(2k-1)x+(k^2-k)=0\) to have both roots positive.
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2-(2k-1)x+(k^2-k)=0\) have both roots positive?
questions.explanation: The sum of the roots is \(2k-1\), and the product is \(k^2-k=k(k-1)\). For both roots to be positive, the sum must be positive, so \(k>\frac{1}{2}\). The product must be positive, so \(k(k-1)>0\), giving \(k<0\) or \(k>1\). Intersecting with \(k>\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(k>1\). The discriminant is \(1\), which is always positive.
questions.hint: Combine the positive-sum and positive-product conditions, and note that the discriminant is always positive.
